_comment: dialog_sized keeps ordinary app windows from matching; every rule also has to survive CONFIRM_SCANS polls (see yolo_watch.py). UserNotificationCenter was the main source of false 'approval needed' alerts, so it is dialog-gated too.
_auto_approve: auto_approve clicks the dialog's Allow/OK button and pushes an after-the-fact alert naming what was granted. It only ever clicks a button whose exact title is in ALLOW_BUTTONS, needs Accessibility permission, and is switched off by `touch ~/.yolo_mode_no_autoapprove` or the menubar toggle.
_auth_fill: auth_fill types the Mac login password (op://Bots/Mac login/password, scripts/mac_password.py) into a macOS auth prompt and presses the window's own default button -- 'Add Helper', 'Modify Settings', whatever Return would press. It fires on every SecurityAgent prompt, not an allowlist of apps: Nathan chose that on 2026-08-04 on the understanding that the high-priority Pushover -- sent after the fact, naming the app and quoting the dialog -- is the review step, so the alert must never be skipped. Two attempts per dialog per run, because a wrong password leaves the same dialog up and an uncapped retry loop locks the account. Off with `touch ~/.yolo_mode_no_password`. This is the one rule that hands out privilege rather than granting a capability: anything that can raise a password prompt now gets admin without a human present, which is the trade being made deliberately.
_catch_all: The last rule is a catch-all: any dialog-shaped window showing an Allow/OK button gets approved, whoever owns it. owner_not carves out the three kinds that stay manual. SecurityAgent, loginwindow and Keychain are how macOS asks Nathan to prove he is Nathan -- a watcher that clicks those turns his password prompt into a formality for whatever asked. 1Password releases vault secrets, so it stays manual EXCEPT the explicit 'Access Requested / Allow ... to get CLI access' dialog, which is auto-Authorized by its own rule above (buttons=['Authorize'] only, so Unlock and other 1Password prompts are untouched). That rule carries no title_any on purpose: the dialog's window title is just '1Password', not 'Access Requested' -- the visible heading lives in a static text inside the web view, not in the title bar. It was matched by title once and silently stopped firing (every `op` call hung to 'authorization timeout' from ~2026-08-04), so the gate is now the button title alone, which is the check that was doing the real work anyway. That did not work either, and on 2026-08-19 the reason was measured: 1Password draws the dialog in a web view, and WebKit publishes nothing to the accessibility API until a client sets AXManualAccessibility on the app. The window read back as one empty AXGroup with no buttons at any depth, so there was never a button to click. The watcher now sets that flag the first time it sees each 1Password process (MANUAL_AX_OWNERS in yolo_watch.py) and the Authorize button appears. It has to be set before the dialog is built -- a dialog already on screen stays blank -- so the rule leads with default_key='first': the dialog takes focus and makes Authorize its default button, so one Return answers it in milliseconds, and the accessibility walk is only the fallback. That keystroke is fenced in three ways: an `op` process must be alive and waiting, 1Password must be frontmost, and its focused window must be the 400x325 dialog. The Unlock and agentic-autofill prompts are other sizes and are raised without `op` running, so they stay manual as before. CoreServicesUIAgent is Gatekeeper, where the Allow-shaped button runs a program that was just downloaded, which is how a drive-by download becomes a running program. Everything else -- screen recording, mic, camera, files, automation, Shortcuts -- is auto-approved. The ScreenCaptureKit picker-bypass alert ("X is requesting to bypass the system private window picker and directly access your screen and audio") needs no rule of its own: it is a UserNotificationCenter dialog with an Allow button, so the rule above already clicks it -- confirmed in the log 2026-07-24 for both Claude and YOLO Mode itself. max_depth stays at the default 3 on purpose. Raising it to 8 was tried the same day and reverted: a single Terminal window yielded 200+ untitled buttons per probe, which is the loop starvation the depth limit exists to prevent.
_turnstile: Cloudflare Turnstile auto-solver (scripts/turnstile.py), merged in from the standalone turnstile-autosolve. Nothing is captured unless a CDP port reports an interstitial or a browser is already frontmost. Needs Screen Recording granted to YOLO Mode. Pause it alone with ~/.turnstile_autosolve_off; the global pause and the auto-approve toggle also stop it.
